title: Peak event selection gives lower next-day wind changes in Atlantic rapid-intensification storms from 1982 to 2023
abstract: We tested how event selection changes estimates of weakening after rapid intensification in Atlantic storms from 1982 to 2023. We used NOAA HURDAT2 and compared the first 24-hour wind gain of at least 30 knots with the peak gain in each storm. In 181 storms with follow-up data for both events, mean wind change in the next 24 hours was +4.92 knots after the first event and -13.81 knots after the peak event. The paired difference was -18.73 knots, with a 95% year-bootstrap interval of -24.14 to -13.83 knots. The rapid-weakening fraction rose from 13.26% to 25.41% under peak selection. The difference persisted with higher gain thresholds and in records with no marked landfall. These results show that event selection changes the estimated next-day outcome. The peak rule uses the full storm record and selects a different life stage. This test does not identify a physical cause of weakening or an effect of ocean warming. The bundle includes the exact raw source, code, derived evidence, and independent checks.

display.caption: Next-day wind change after the first and peak RI events in the same Atlantic storms, 1982 to 2023. The middle panel gives paired differences and 95% intervals from resampling years. A negative value means less gain or more weakening after peak selection. Landfall is screened with the L record marker only.
